title: Buddhist Kathmandu: Boudha to Namobuddha
meta_description: 5 nights on the Buddhist trail of the Kathmandu Valley: dawn kora at Boudha, Swayambhu, Patan's monastery courtyards, the Pharping caves and Namobuddha.
summary: Five nights following the Buddhist thread of the Kathmandu Valley: three at Boudhanath for dawn koras and monastery visits, Swayambhu and the Newar Buddhist courtyards of Patan, a night in Pharping near the caves where Guru Rinpoche meditated, and a last day at the hilltop stupa of Namobuddha.
intro: Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley has two faces, and this journey shows both. One is Newar Buddhism, practised for well over a thousand years in the courtyard monasteries of Patan and Kathmandu by families of Bajracharya priests and Shakya craftsmen. The other is Tibetan, which grew around Boudhanath and Pharping after 1959, when refugees from Tibet settled here and rebuilt monasteries of every school. Both still share the same stupas, festivals and pilgrims, and you will often see a Newar priest and a Tibetan monk at the same shrine on the same morning.

We base you for three nights at the Hyatt Regency, a ten-minute walk from the Boudha stupa, so you can join the kora at dawn and again at dusk. A guide who knows both traditions explains the rituals without lecturing, and arranges visits to monasteries at prayer times. The pace is slow on purpose: there is time to sit, light butter lamps and watch. Expect early starts on two mornings, and afternoons that are yours.
story: The journey begins in circles. At Boudhanath, Tibetan grandmothers walk around the white dome before sunrise with prayer beads in hand, and you walk with them. Swayambhu tells the valley's oldest Buddhist story, of a lotus that bloomed on a lake and a bodhisattva who drained the water to let people reach it. In Patan you step through low doorways into courtyards where Newar Buddhist families have kept their shrines for centuries. Then the road climbs south to Pharping, where Guru Rinpoche is said to have reached realisation in a cave on the hillside, and where monasteries crowd the slope. The last day crosses the valley to Namobuddha, the hill where, the Jataka says, a prince gave his body to a starving tigress.
highlights: Dawn and dusk kora around Boudhanath with Tibetan families
Morning prayers at a Boudha monastery and the hilltop Kopan monastery
Swayambhu and the Newar Buddhist courtyards of Patan, including the Golden Temple
The Asura and Yanglesho caves of Pharping, sacred to Guru Rinpoche
The Namobuddha stupa and Thrangu Tashi Yangtse monastery

days.title: Arrive at Boudha, first evening kora
days.text: We meet you at the airport and drive the short distance to the Hyatt Regency, set in large gardens near Boudhanath. Rest, then walk with your guide to the stupa as the evening kora fills. Monks, families and old couples walk clockwise around the dome, spinning prayer wheels set into the outer wall and murmuring om mani padme hum. Your guide explains what the stupa's levels and the painted eyes stand for. Light a row of butter lamps at one of the lamp houses, then eat Tibetan thukpa and momo at a rooftop restaurant facing the stupa.

days.title: Dawn at Boudha and the hill of Kopan
days.text: Walk to the stupa before sunrise, when the kora is busiest and the lanes smell of juniper smoke. After breakfast visit Shechen, a large Nyingma monastery behind the stupa, and sit quietly at the back during morning prayers if they are on. Later drive up to Kopan Monastery on its hill north of Boudha, a Gelug monastery known for its meditation courses for visitors. Walk its gardens and look back across the valley. The afternoon is free for rest or for the thangka painting schools around Boudha, where students spend years learning the proportions of each deity.

days.title: Swayambhu and Patan's Buddhist courtyards
days.text: Early drive to Swayambhunath on its wooded hill. Walk the circuit of prayer wheels, see the great vajra at the top of the eastern stairs and the shrine to Harati, protector of children. Your guide tells the Swayambhu Purana story of Manjushri draining the valley lake. Then cross to Patan, where Newar Buddhism lives in bahals, monastery courtyards inside the city. Visit Kwa Bahal, the Golden Temple, with its gilded roofs and resident child priest, Uku Bahal and the terracotta Mahaboudha. Lunch in Patan and return to Boudha for the evening kora.

days.title: Chobhar gorge and the caves of Pharping
days.text: Drive south to Chobhar, the narrow gorge where the Bagmati leaves the valley, which the Swayambhu Purana says Manjushri cut with his sword. Continue up to Pharping. Climb to the Asura Cave, a small rock shelter where Guru Rinpoche is said to have meditated and where pilgrims touch his handprint in the stone. Walk on to Yanglesho, the cave below Shesh Narayan where Tibetan tradition says he attained realisation. Visit the Newar Vajrayogini temple on the hill and spend the evening at your guesthouse among monasteries, listening to horns and drums at dusk.

days.title: Across the valley to Namobuddha
days.text: Leave Pharping after morning prayers and drive across the valley and out along the Araniko Highway, then up a winding hill road to Namobuddha at about 1,750 m. Walk around the stupa, then climb the short path to the stone tablet that shows Prince Mahasattva offering himself to the tigress. Above it stands Thrangu Tashi Yangtse monastery, where young monks study and debate; visitors may watch the afternoon puja from the back of the hall. Drive 45 minutes to Dhulikhel for the night, with views north to the Himalaya.

days.title: Mountain dawn and fly home
days.text: On a clear morning Dhulikhel shows the Himalaya from Langtang to Gaurishankar. After breakfast walk down through the old Newar bazaar, where small pagoda temples and stone water spouts stand among brick houses with carved windows. Then drive back along the Araniko Highway, through Banepa and past Bhaktapur, to Tribhuvan International Airport. If your flight is late, we can stop for an hour at Bhaktapur on the way, or return to Boudha for a final kora.

good_to_know: Walk clockwise around stupas, chortens and prayer wheels, and keep mani stones on your right.
Monastery prayer times change by season and by festival; your guide checks each day.
The Pharping guesthouse is simple and quiet, with basic rooms; it is the setting, not the comfort, that matters.
Kopan Monastery runs residential courses, including a well-known November course; book separately and check current status before you travel.
Losar in February or March and Buddha Jayanti in April or May bring big crowds and ceremonies to Boudha.

faqs.q: What are the main Buddhist sites in the Kathmandu Valley?
faqs.a: The two great stupas, Boudhanath and Swayambhunath, are both UNESCO-listed and both active places of worship. Patan has many Newar Buddhist monastery courtyards, including Kwa Bahal, the Golden Temple. Pharping, south of the city, has caves linked to Guru Rinpoche, and Namobuddha, south-east of Dhulikhel, marks the Jataka story of the prince and the tigress. Kopan and the Boudha monasteries welcome visitors.

faqs.q: Can visitors attend prayers at monasteries in Boudha?
faqs.a: Usually yes, quietly and from the back. Many monasteries around Boudhanath hold morning and late-afternoon prayers, and visitors can sit on the side benches or the floor if the hall is open. Take shoes off, do not point your feet at the altar, do not use flash and ask before photographing monks. Your guide checks which halls are open each day.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Newar and Tibetan Buddhism?
faqs.a: Both are Vajrayana traditions. Newar Buddhism has been practised in the valley for centuries, in Sanskrit, by married Bajracharya priests and Shakya families who look after courtyard monasteries in Patan and Kathmandu. Tibetan Buddhism came in larger numbers after 1959 with refugees from Tibet, who built monasteries of all four main schools around Boudha, Swayambhu and Pharping, with monks and nuns.

faqs.q: Who was Guru Rinpoche and why is Pharping sacred?
faqs.a: Guru Rinpoche, also called Padmasambhava, was the Indian master credited with bringing Vajrayana Buddhism to Tibet in the eighth century. Tibetan tradition says he meditated in the caves of Pharping and attained realisation at Yanglesho before travelling north. Pilgrims visit the Asura Cave, with a handprint said to be his, and Yanglesho below Shesh Narayan.

faqs.q: Can I do a meditation course in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes. Kopan Monastery near Boudha runs introductory courses through the year and a longer residential course, traditionally in November. Other centres around Boudha and Swayambhu offer short sessions and talks. Courses must be booked directly and fill quickly, so check current status before you travel. We can build this journey around your course dates.

faqs.q: How should I behave at a stupa?
faqs.a: Walk clockwise, with the stupa on your right. Spin prayer wheels clockwise too. Do not climb on chortens or sit on mani stone walls. Dress modestly, remove hats inside monasteries and take off shoes when asked. It is fine to light butter lamps and to make a small donation. Ask before photographing people at prayer, especially monks and elderly pilgrims.

faqs.q: When is the best time for a Buddhist pilgrimage to Kathmandu?
faqs.a: October to April is the most comfortable. Losar, the Tibetan New Year in February or March, brings dances and crowds at Boudha. Buddha Jayanti, the full moon of Baisakh in April or May, is celebrated at Swayambhu and Boudha. Monsoon months are wetter but the stupas stay open and fewer tourists visit. Festival dates move each year; check before booking.

faqs.q: Is the Namobuddha visit physically demanding?
faqs.a: Not very. The car drives up to Namobuddha, and from the stupa a stepped path of about 15–20 minutes climbs to the stone tablet and the monastery at the top. The altitude is about 1,750 m, so you may feel a little breathless. If you prefer to walk, we can drop you in Dhulikhel and you can hike there in 3–4 hours on farm trails.

faqs.q: Where should I stay in Boudha?
faqs.a: The Hyatt Regency Kathmandu is the most comfortable choice, ten minutes on foot from the stupa, with large gardens. There are also many simple guesthouses in the lanes around the stupa, some run by monasteries, which put you closer to the kora but have basic rooms. Staying in Boudha rather than Thamel lets you walk to the stupa before dawn.
